title: HELOC Calculator: Home Equity Line Payment & Available Credit
description: Estimate your HELOC payment and how much you can borrow. See your interest-only draw-period payment, the amortizing repayment payment, available credit at 85% CLTV, and total interest.
answerSnippet: A HELOC (home equity line of credit) has two phases. During the draw period (often 10 years) you typically pay interest only — your balance times the monthly rate — so a $50,000 balance at 8.5% costs about $354 a month. During the repayment period (often 20 years) the balance amortizes, raising the payment (to about $434 a month in that example). How much you can borrow is roughly your home value times the lender's combined loan-to-value limit (commonly 85%) minus your current mortgage. This calculator estimates all three: available credit, interest-only payment, and repayment payment.
intro:
A **HELOC (Home Equity Line of Credit)** lets you borrow against your home's equity like a credit card: a revolving line you can draw from as needed. But its payment structure trips up many borrowers, because it changes partway through. This calculator estimates the two payments you need to plan for — plus **how much you can actually borrow**.

A HELOC has two phases. During the **draw period** (commonly **10 years**) you can borrow and repay freely, and lenders usually require only **interest-only** payments — low, but they don't reduce the balance. When the draw period ends, the **repayment period** (commonly **20 years**) begins: no more borrowing, and your payment jumps because it now includes **principal**. Many borrowers are surprised by that increase.

Enter your **home value**, **current mortgage balance**, the **HELOC balance** you plan to carry, and the **rate**. The tool estimates your **available credit** (based on the lender's combined loan-to-value limit, typically 85%), your **interest-only draw payment**, your **amortizing repayment payment**, and the **total interest** over the life of the line.
keyTakeaway: A HELOC has a low **interest-only draw period** (balance × monthly rate) then a higher **amortizing repayment period**. Available credit ≈ **home value × CLTV limit (often 85%) − mortgage balance**. On $50,000 at 8.5%, the payment jumps from about **$354** (interest-only) to about **$434** (repayment). HELOC rates are usually **variable**, so payments can rise.

explanation:
## How a HELOC payment works

```
Available credit    = Home value × CLTV limit − mortgage balance
Draw period payment = Balance × (APR ÷ 12)            (interest only)
Repayment payment   = Balance amortized over the repayment term (principal + interest)
```

The draw-period payment is low because you are only covering interest — the balance does not shrink. When repayment begins, principal is added and the payment rises, sometimes sharply.

## The two phases of a HELOC

| Phase | Typical length | Payment | Can you borrow? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Draw period | ~10 years | Interest only (low) | Yes, up to your limit |
| Repayment period | ~20 years | Principal + interest (higher) | No |

## Worked example — the payment jump

A $50,000 balance at 8.5%:
- **Draw period:** $50,000 × 8.5% ÷ 12 = **$354/month** (interest only).
- **Repayment period (20 yr):** amortizing the same $50,000 = **$434/month**.
- That is an **$80/month jump** — and if you had drawn more, or rates rose, the increase would be larger.

## How much can you borrow?

Lenders cap your **combined loan-to-value (CLTV)** — your first mortgage plus the HELOC — usually around **85%** of the home's value (some go to 90%).

| Home value | Mortgage | 85% CLTV limit | Available HELOC |
|---|---|---|---|
| $400,000 | $250,000 | $340,000 | $90,000 |
| $500,000 | $300,000 | $425,000 | $125,000 |
| $600,000 | $200,000 | $510,000 | $310,000 |

## Watch-outs before you draw

- **Variable rate:** Most HELOCs are tied to the prime rate, so your payment can rise (or fall) as rates move. Budget for higher rates.
- **Payment shock:** Plan now for the repayment-period increase, especially if you carry a large balance to the end of the draw period.
- **Your home is collateral:** A HELOC is secured by your house — default can lead to foreclosure. Borrow conservatively.
- **Interest deductibility:** HELOC interest is only tax-deductible if the funds are used to **buy, build, or substantially improve** the home securing the loan, and only if you itemize.

## Disclaimer

Educational estimate. Actual HELOC terms — draw and repayment lengths, CLTV limits, margins, rate caps, and fees — vary by lender, and rates are typically variable. This tool models principal and interest only. Confirm figures with your lender.

faq.q: How is a HELOC payment calculated?
faq.a: During the **draw period**, most HELOCs require interest only: **balance × (APR ÷ 12)**. So a $50,000 balance at 8.5% is about **$354/month**. During the **repayment period**, the balance amortizes over the remaining term, adding principal and raising the payment (to about **$434/month** in that example).

faq.q: How much can I borrow with a HELOC?
faq.a: Lenders limit your **combined loan-to-value (CLTV)** — first mortgage plus HELOC — usually to about **85%** of your home's value. So available credit ≈ **home value × 85% − mortgage balance**. On a $500,000 home with a $300,000 mortgage, that is roughly **$125,000**.

faq.q: What is the difference between the draw and repayment periods?
faq.a: The **draw period** (typically 10 years) is when you can borrow and usually pay interest only. The **repayment period** (typically 20 years) begins after — you can no longer borrow, and your payment rises because it now includes **principal**. The transition often causes a noticeable payment increase.

faq.q: Why does my HELOC payment go up later?
faq.a: Because interest-only draw-period payments don't reduce the balance. When repayment starts, the **entire balance must be paid off over the remaining term**, so principal is added to every payment. If you carried a large balance, the jump can be significant — plan for it in advance.

faq.q: Is a HELOC rate fixed or variable?
faq.a: Most HELOCs have a **variable rate** tied to the prime rate plus a margin, so your payment can change as rates move. Some lenders offer a fixed-rate conversion option for part of your balance. Because rates vary, budget for the possibility of higher payments.

faq.q: HELOC vs home equity loan — what's the difference?
faq.a: A **home equity loan** gives you a lump sum at a **fixed rate** with fixed payments. A **HELOC** is a revolving **line** you draw from as needed, usually at a **variable rate** with interest-only draw payments. A HELOC offers flexibility; a home equity loan offers payment certainty.

Only if you use the money to **buy, build, or substantially improve the home** that secures the HELOC — and only if you itemize deductions. Interest on a HELOC used for other purposes (paying off cards, a car, tuition) is **not** deductible under current federal rules.

faq.q: Can I lose my home with a HELOC?
faq.a: Yes — a HELOC is **secured by your home**, so defaulting can lead to foreclosure, just like a first mortgage. Because it puts your home at risk and payments can rise, borrow only what you can comfortably repay even if rates increase.
